prompt: EHR Healthcare runs an open-source Prometheus server and Grafana in each of its Kubernetes clusters, one per environment and region. Alertmanager emails every firing rule to one shared mailbox, and staff routinely ignore the messages. Leadership wants a single place to see performance and usage across all clusters, wants to keep the team's existing PromQL rules and Grafana dashboards, and wants to stop operating Prometheus servers. Which approach should the architect recommend?

choices.text: Keep each Prometheus server and point Alertmanager at a Pub/Sub topic instead of the mailbox, so the same rules notify a different destination
choices.rationale: Changing the destination does not reduce alert volume or make the alerts actionable, and the per-cluster servers still have to be run and queried separately. It addresses neither the visibility nor the administration goals.

choices.text: Federate every cluster's Prometheus into one central Prometheus server on a Compute Engine VM and route its Alertmanager to a chat channel
choices.rationale: Federation gives one view, but EHR would now operate and scale a central server that is a single point of failure, which conflicts with the goal of no longer running Prometheus servers.

choices.text: Rewrite every alert rule as a log-based metric in Cloud Logging and retire PromQL and the Grafana dashboards after the cutover
choices.rationale: Log-based metrics are for signals that exist in logs. Rewriting every rule throws away the team's PromQL rules and dashboards, which the requirements explicitly say to keep.

choices.text: Adopt Managed Service for Prometheus with managed collection, move the rules to PromQL alerting policies, and page only on urgent alerts
choices.rationale: Managed collection removes the servers, the global backend allows PromQL queries across clusters and projects, and Grafana dashboards keep working. Prometheus alerting rules can migrate to Cloud Monitoring policies and channels, so urgent alerts are separated from noise.

explanation: Managed Service for Prometheus keeps the Prometheus data model, PromQL and Grafana while Google runs the collection and storage backend. Moving rules into Cloud Monitoring alerting policies puts alerting and notification channels in one place, where urgent alerts can go to a paging channel and the rest to lower-urgency channels.

prompt: An online ticketing company writes its checkout API request logs to a project-level, unlocked log bucket. The SRE team must report average latency per endpoint, grouped by hour, over the retained history, and wants to run ad hoc SQL against it. Platform leadership will not pay for a second copy of the logs or accept a new export pipeline to maintain. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Upgrade the existing log bucket to Observability Analytics (formerly Log Analytics) and run SQL that groups entries by endpoint and hour
choices.rationale: Correct. Upgrading a project-level, unlocked bucket enables SQL grouping and aggregation over the logs where they already sit. No sink or copy is needed, and Logs Explorer keeps working on the same bucket.

choices.text: Query the bucket in Logs Explorer with the Logging query language and compute the hourly averages from its histogram panel
choices.rationale: Logs Explorer is built for troubleshooting and filtering. It does not support aggregate operations such as grouping and averaging, and its histogram shows entry counts, not latency means.

choices.text: Create a log sink that exports the checkout logs to BigQuery tables and run the hourly aggregations on that exported dataset
choices.rationale: This works technically but is the pattern leadership ruled out: the sink duplicates the data into a second store with its own storage cost, plus a pipeline to maintain. A linked dataset on an upgraded bucket gives BigQuery access without a copy.

choices.text: Define a distribution log-based metric on the latency field and chart the hourly mean per endpoint in Cloud Monitoring
choices.rationale: A user-defined log-based metric is fed only by entries received after it is created, so it cannot answer for the retained history. It is also a fixed, predefined aggregation, not ad hoc SQL.

explanation: When the need is aggregation and trends over logs you already store, enable analytics on the log bucket rather than exporting. Keep Logs Explorer for filtering and troubleshooting individual entries.

prompt: A logistics company ships to a production GKE cluster through a Cloud Build and Cloud Deploy pipeline. Last month an engineer built a hotfix image on a laptop, pushed it to Artifact Registry and applied the Deployment with kubectl. It skipped the staging integration tests and caused an outage. Production must now run only images that the pipeline built and that passed the staging integration suite, even if someone applies manifests directly to the cluster. On-call must still be able to ship an emergency fix, with a clear audit trail. What should the architect do?

choices.text: Enforce a Binary Authorization policy on production requiring a pipeline-signed attestation for the image digest after staging tests pass, with audited break-glass
choices.rationale: Correct. The pipeline signs an attestation for the image digest only after the staging suite succeeds, and the admission check blocks anything without it, including direct kubectl applies. Break-glass is the sanctioned override and every use is written to Cloud Audit Logs.

choices.text: Restrict Artifact Registry push access to the Cloud Build service account, deploy to production by release tag, and grant on-call engineers a separate emergency push role
choices.rationale: Registry permissions show who pushed an image, not that it passed the staging tests. Tags are mutable, anyone with cluster access can still apply any image the registry holds, and the emergency push role reopens the original hole without a dedicated audit trail.

choices.text: Enable Artifact Analysis vulnerability scanning on the repository and have the release process refuse to promote any image whose scan reports a critical or high severity vulnerability
choices.rationale: A clean scan says nothing about whether the integration suite ran. The check lives in the release process, so a direct kubectl apply of the hotfix image still bypasses it, and there is no emergency path.

choices.text: Add a manual approval to the Cloud Deploy promotion into production so that a second engineer must approve each release before it rolls out to the cluster
choices.rationale: An approval gate only governs releases that flow through Cloud Deploy. The hotfix reached the cluster through kubectl and never touched the pipeline. A human approval also proves nothing about test results.

explanation: Pipeline-side controls only protect the paths that go through the pipeline. Enforcing at deploy time on the cluster, with attestations bound to image digests, closes the bypass, and break-glass keeps emergencies possible and auditable.

prompt: A retailer lifts and shifts a Java order service onto a managed instance group of Compute Engine VMs built from a custom image. In Cloud Monitoring the CPU and network charts populate, but the memory and disk-space utilization charts show no data. The application writes logs to files under /var/log/orders/, and none of them appear in Cloud Logging. The team needs to alert on memory and search those logs without changing application code. What should they do?

choices.text: Install the Ops Agent on the instances, for example through an agent policy, and configure it to read the application log files
choices.rationale: Correct. Memory, disk and process metrics from inside the guest come only from the Ops Agent, which also tails log files at paths you configure. An agent policy installs it across the fleet without touching the application.

choices.text: Turn on the detailed monitoring option for the instance group so that the platform publishes guest-level memory and disk metrics
choices.rationale: Compute Engine has no such switch. The platform reports basic hypervisor-level metrics such as CPU and network, and memory and process utilization are available only when an agent runs inside the VM.

choices.text: Grant the instances' service account the Monitoring Viewer and Logs Viewer roles so the VMs can read their own metrics and log files
choices.rationale: Viewer roles allow reading data that already exists in Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging. Nothing collects or sends guest data without an agent, and a sender needs the writer roles instead (Logs Writer and Monitoring Metric Writer).

choices.text: Add the Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring client libraries to the service so it emits memory gauges and its own log entries directly
choices.rationale: This can work for a codebase the team is free to change, but the requirement rules out code changes. It would also miss disk and OS-level data and leave the existing log files unread.

explanation: Hypervisor-level metrics cover CPU and network only. For guest memory, disk space, processes and file-based logs on Compute Engine, run the Ops Agent and roll it out fleet-wide with an agent policy or automation.
